name: Modern Day

worldBrief:
# The world on 1 January 2026

**Russia-Ukraine.** The war is nearly four years old. Russia holds about a fifth of Ukraine, including Crimea, most of Luhansk and much of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts. Its slow, costly offensive grinds forward around Pokrovsk, Huliaipole and toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. Ukraine strikes Russian refineries, ports and the shadow tanker fleet with long-range drones; Russia pounds Ukraine's power grid. From November 2025 the Trump administration pushed a peace plan, first drafted with Russian input and then revised with Kyiv and the Europeans. The sticking points are Russia's demand for the rest of Donetsk, limits on Ukraine's army, NATO non-membership, and what security guarantees the US and a European "coalition of the willing" (led by the UK and France) would give. The EU agreed to fund Ukraine for 2026-27 with a large joint loan after failing to agree on using frozen Russian assets. A corruption scandal around the state nuclear company cost Zelensky his chief of staff. No ceasefire is in force.

**Middle East.** A US-brokered ceasefire in Gaza has held loosely since 10 October 2025. All living hostages were released; Israel still controls roughly half the Strip behind the "yellow line". UN Security Council Resolution 2803 endorsed a Board of Peace and an International Stabilization Force, but no troop contributor will fight Hamas, which refuses to disarm. Strikes and killings continue on both sides. Israel also keeps striking Hezbollah in Lebanon, where the government is trying to disarm the group, and holds positions in southern Syria. In June 2025 Israel and then the US struck Iran's nuclear and missile sites in a 12-day war. Iran's enrichment programme is badly damaged but its stockpile of highly enriched uranium is unaccounted for. In September the E3 triggered the snapback of UN sanctions, which Russia and China call illegal. Iran's currency is collapsing, and it faces water shortages and power cuts. Israel goes to elections by October 2026.

**Syria** is ruled by President Ahmed al-Sharaa, who visited the White House and joined the anti-ISIS coalition. Most US, EU and UK sanctions have been lifted, and the Caesar Act was repealed in December 2025. Integration of the Kurdish-led SDF has stalled, and sectarian massacres of Alawites and Druze in 2025 left deep distrust.

**Africa.** In Sudan the RSF captured El Fasher in October 2025 amid mass killings and now holds almost all of Darfur, while fighting moves into Kordofan. The army government sits in Port Sudan and Khartoum. Famine is widespread, and the UAE is accused of arming the RSF. In eastern DR Congo the M23, backed by Rwanda, still holds Goma and Bukavu despite a US-brokered DRC-Rwanda peace agreement (signed in Washington in June and December 2025) and a Doha framework with M23; fighting continues. The juntas of Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger have left ECOWAS, formed the Alliance of Sahel States and expelled French forces. They rely on Russian partners while jihadists blockade Bamako's fuel supply. In late 2025 coups took power in Madagascar and Guinea-Bissau, and a coup attempt in Benin failed. Ethiopia-Eritrea tension is high over Ethiopia's push for sea access.

**Americas.** The US has massed warships in the Caribbean, struck dozens of alleged drug boats since September 2025, designated the Cartel de los Soles a terrorist organisation and is pressing Maduro to go. Venezuela is under blockade-like pressure, and a war or a regime collapse is possible. Relations with Colombia's Petro are hostile. Argentina's Milei won the October midterms with US financial backing. Chile elected José Antonio Kast, Bolivia elected Rodrigo Paz, and Honduras elected Nasry Asfura, all on the right. Brazil votes in October 2026.

**Asia.** China and Japan are in their worst spat in years after PM Sanae Takaichi said a Taiwan contingency could threaten Japan's survival. Beijing responded with travel warnings, a seafood ban and military pressure. The PLA keeps up large exercises around Taiwan. The US and China agreed a one-year trade truce in Kuala Lumpur and Busan (October-November 2025): tariff cuts, a pause on rare-earth export controls and soybean purchases. India and Pakistan fought a four-day air and missile conflict in May 2025 after the Pahalgam attack; the ceasefire holds, but there is no dialogue. Thailand and Cambodia fought border battles in July and December 2025 despite a peace accord signed with Trump in October. Myanmar's junta is holding phased elections from 28 December 2025, widely seen as a sham, while losing ground to resistance armies. Pakistan has clashed with the Afghan Taliban across their border.

**Caucasus.** Armenia and Azerbaijan initialled a peace agreement at the White House in August 2025, including a US-run transit route through southern Armenia (the "Trump Route", TRIPP). The final treaty awaits Armenian constitutional change.

**Trade and economy.** US tariffs are at their highest level since the 1930s: a 10% baseline, high "reciprocal" rates and sectoral duties on steel, cars and other goods. Deals with the EU, UK, Japan, Korea, Vietnam and others reduced rates in exchange for investment pledges. The Supreme Court has heard the challenge to the emergency (IEEPA) tariffs but not yet ruled. Global growth is about 3%, carried by a huge AI investment boom that has driven up US stock valuations amid bubble fears. Inflation has mostly eased but remains sticky in the US and UK; the Fed has cut rates to 3.5-3.75%. Oil is cheap (Brent around $60) as OPEC+ unwinds cuts. Gold is at record highs and China's exports are at a record surplus. Debt burdens in France, the UK and the US worry markets.

# Simulation rules: Modern Day (2026)

**Realism first.** Outcomes follow how the world actually works in 2026. A single turn rarely changes much. Big shifts need sustained effort, allies and luck.

**Nuclear deterrence.** Nine states have nuclear weapons. No one invades a nuclear power's core territory or tries to topple its regime by force without facing escalation risks that leaders treat as unacceptable. Nuclear powers fight through proxies, sanctions, cyber operations and limited strikes. Any nuclear use is a world-changing event with enormous political, economic and humanitarian consequences.

**Wars are slow and costly.** Modern militaries with drones, missiles and dense defences advance slowly, often only a few kilometres a month. Offensives burn equipment, ammunition and manpower. War exhaustion rises, economies suffer, and outside powers resupply the weaker side. Quick, decisive conquest is the exception and usually requires overwhelming superiority against a weak, isolated target.

**Economic interdependence.** Supply chains (chips, rare earths, energy, food) bind rivals together. Tariffs, export controls and sanctions hurt the imposer as well as the target. Markets react within days, and capital flight, currency crises and inflation follow reckless policy.

**Sanctions bite gradually.** They raise costs and erode growth over months and years. They rarely change a regime's behaviour quickly, and evasion through third countries is common. Coalitions matter more than unilateral measures.

**Domestic politics matter.** Elections, coalition arithmetic, courts, protests and elite factions constrain every government. Democracies face scheduled elections that can replace leaders and change course. Autocracies fear unrest, elite splits and economic collapse. Unpopular wars and austerity cost support.

**Diplomacy and institutions.** Alliances, treaties and organisations shape behaviour. The UN Security Council is limited by vetoes. EU and NATO decisions need consensus or large majorities. Leaders weigh credibility, reputation and precedent.

**Information environment.** Disinformation, social media and leaks shape opinion quickly. Atrocities and blunders are seen worldwide. Narratives can rally or erode support.

**Plausibility.** Countries act according to their interests, capabilities and leaders' personalities. Surprises happen, such as coups, disasters, assassinations and market crashes, but they should be rooted in existing tensions.

formables.name: United Korea
formables.concept: The two Korean states become one country again, by agreement or by force.

formables.name: Gran Colombia
formables.concept: Bolívar's republic of the northern Andes and the isthmus is restored as one federal state.

formables.name: Federal Republic of Central America
formables.concept: The five republics of the isthmus rejoin the federation they formed after independence from Spain.

formables.name: United Provinces of the Río de la Plata
formables.concept: The lands of the old Spanish viceroyalty of the River Plate unite under Buenos Aires again.

formables.name: Union of South American Nations
formables.concept: All twelve South American republics merge into one continental federation with a single parliament and currency.

formables.name: West Indies Federation
formables.concept: The English-speaking Caribbean islands revive the short-lived federation of 1958-1962.

formables.name: United Ireland
formables.concept: Northern Ireland leaves the United Kingdom and joins the Republic, making the whole island one state.

formables.name: Kalmar Union
formables.concept: Denmark, Norway and Sweden join under one crown again, as in the medieval Kalmar Union.

formables.name: Nordic Federation
formables.concept: The five Nordic states pool their defence, currency and foreign policy in a single federation.

formables.name: Baltic Federation
formables.concept: Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania merge into one federal state on the Baltic coast.

formables.name: Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth
formables.concept: Poland and Lithuania revive their old union as one Commonwealth of two nations.

formables.name: Intermarium
formables.concept: A federation of the lands between the Baltic and the Black Sea, led by Poland and Ukraine, in the spirit of Piłsudski's plan.

formables.name: Union State of Russia and Belarus
formables.concept: The 1999 Union State treaty is carried through into a real single state with one government.

formables.name: Greater Romania
formables.concept: Romania and Moldova unite, as Romanian and Moldovan unionists propose.

formables.name: Czechoslovakia
formables.concept: The Czech Republic and Slovakia undo the 1993 split and become one federal state again.

formables.name: Austria-Hungary
formables.concept: Austria and Hungary rebuild their dual union as a modern two-part federation.

formables.name: Danubian Federation
formables.concept: The states of the middle Danube form a federation of equals, as liberal reformers proposed before 1914.

formables.name: Yugoslavia
formables.concept: The former Yugoslav republics reunite in a new South Slav federation.

formables.name: Balkan Federation
formables.concept: Yugoslavia, Bulgaria and Albania join in the Balkan federation Tito and Dimitrov discussed in 1947.

formables.name: Benelux Union
formables.concept: Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg turn their customs union into one federal state.

formables.name: Iberian Union
formables.concept: Spain and Portugal join as one federation covering the whole peninsula.

formables.name: European Federation
formables.concept: The European Union becomes a single federal state with one government, army and foreign policy.

formables.name: United Cyprus
formables.concept: The Republic of Cyprus and the Turkish Cypriot north agree to reunite the island in a bicommunal federation.

formables.name: Albania-Kosovo Union
formables.concept: Albania and Kosovo merge by referendum into one Albanian state.

formables.name: Transcaucasian Federation
formables.concept: Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan revive the short-lived 1918 South Caucasus federation.

formables.name: Central Asian Union
formables.concept: The five Central Asian republics unite, as Kazakhstan proposed in 2005.

formables.name: Indochinese Federation
formables.concept: Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia form one federation across the Mekong lands.

formables.name: Federation of Malaysia
formables.concept: Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei form the wider Malaysia planned in 1963.

formables.name: United Arab Republic
formables.concept: Egypt and Syria restore Nasser's 1958 union as one republic.

formables.name: Federation of Arab Republics
formables.concept: Egypt, Libya and Syria form the federation they founded in 1972, with real common institutions this time.

formables.name: United Arab Nation
formables.concept: One Arab state from the Atlantic to the Gulf, the pan-Arab dream of Nasserists and Ba'athists.

formables.name: Gulf Union
formables.concept: The six Gulf Cooperation Council monarchies merge into one union, as Saudi Arabia proposed in 2011.

formables.name: Maghreb Union
formables.concept: The states of North Africa's west turn the Arab Maghreb Union into one political union.

formables.name: Greater Somalia
formables.concept: All the Somali-inhabited lands of the Horn of Africa unite under one Somali state, the five points of the Somali star.

formables.name: East African Federation
formables.concept: The core East African Community states carry out their long-planned political federation.

formables.name: Mali Federation
formables.concept: Senegal and Mali re-form the federation they founded at independence in 1959-1960.

formables.name: Confederation of Sahel States
formables.concept: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger turn their 2024 confederation into one united Sahelian state.
